:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = e^{x - y}\,.
$$

The right-hand side is a function of both $x$ and $y,$ so we can't solve the equation by integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ at least not straight away. So, how do we find a general solution to the equation?

First of all, note that it is possible to separate the variables $x$ and $y$ on each side of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x-y}=\frac{{e}^{x}}{{e}^{y}}\,⟹\,{e}^{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the rule for integration by substitution, we can simplify the integrand on the left-hand side and carry out the integration as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & ={e}^{x}+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
e^y  	= e^x + C.
$$

This is an **implicit form** of the solution since it is not written explicitly as $y=y(x).$

We can write our general solution in **explicit form** (i.e., in the form $y=y(x)$) by noting that since $e^y > 0$ for all $y$, we may assume that the right-hand side is positive and apply the natural logarithm, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}({e}^{x}+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}({e}^{x}+C)\end{aligned}
$$

The differential equation that we just solved was **separable**. A first-order differential equation is separable if it can be written in the form

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} = h(x)g(y).
$$

If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are *separated* when it is written in the form

$$
\dfrac{1}{g(y)} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = h(x).
$$

Once the variables are separated, we can integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{g(y)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int h(x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}y}{g(y)} & =\int h(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We then evaluate both integrals and find the solution. Note that for the solution to be valid, we require $g(y)\neq 0.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y' = \dfrac {x^2}{y}.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{y} \\ y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\text{d}y & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}y^2 = \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 + C.
$$

We can express the solution in the form $y = y(x)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+C \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+2C \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+2C} \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+K}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K = 2C.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Finding a General Solution in Explicit Form

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y' + 2xy = 0$ for $y\neq 0.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}+2xy & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2xy \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =-2\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-{x}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\ln \vert y \vert = -x^2 + C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y = y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-{x}^{2}+C \\ |y| & ={e}^{-{x}^{2}+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{-{x}^{2}}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K = e^C$  and $K > 0.$ 

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y = Ke^{-x^2}.
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Given that $x,y \geq 0,$ separate the variables in the following differential equation: 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \sqrt{2xy}
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
A differentiable equation is *separable* if it can be written in the form

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = h(x)g(y).
$$

If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are *separated* when it is written in the form

$$
\dfrac{1}{g(y)} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = h(x).
$$

Notice that our differentiable equation is separable since it can be written as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} =  \sqrt{2x} \cdot  \sqrt{y}.
$$

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y}} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} = \sqrt{2x}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Separating the Variables in a Differential Equation

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x}{y} \\ y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\,\text{d}y & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+K \\ {y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+2K \\ {y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C= 2K.$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
y^2 = x^2 + C .
$$
